extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literary criticism and rhetoric; writers interested in narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Wayne C. Booth's theoretical criteria for analyzing and producing fiction and rhetoric — including implied authorship, narrator reliability, rhetorical 'lines of interest', and the ethical obligations of rhetors. Useful for evaluating how narrative choices persuade readers and shape meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative as a form of rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: All narrative is a form of rhetoric; narrative choices are rhetorical acts intended to persuade or guide readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booth argues that authors invariably both show and tell, and that attempts to dichotomize 'showing' versus 'telling' are simplistic and flawed. Evaluate narratives by how they use rhetorical means to convey their various 'commitments' and to persuade readers along chosen lines of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied author (author's 'second self')
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers infer an implied author — an ideal, literary, created version of the real author — from the text; this implied author embodies choices, commitments, beliefs, and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the implied author as the sum of an author's textual choices; readers construct a picture of this official scribe who will never be neutral toward all values. The reader's reactions to the implied author's commitments help determine response to the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth coined the term 'unreliable narrator' to describe narrators whose accounts cannot be taken at face value and whose reliability affects how readers interpret the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider degree of narrator reliability (reliable/unreliable) and whether the narrator is personal or impersonal; these qualities shape rhetorical effects, reader inferences about the implied author, and potential pitfalls in commentary or presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Literary Interest (three kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three 'Types of Literary Interest' available for technical manipulation in fiction: (1) Intellectual/cognitive, (2) Qualitative, (3) Practical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Intellectual/cognitive: provoke curiosity about facts, true interpretation, motives, or truth about life. 2) Qualitative: provoke desire to see patterns or forms completed or aesthetic development. 3) Practical: provoke desire for the success/failure or change in characters. Evaluate and design fiction by choosing and manipulating these interests to achieve intended reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lines of interest and rhetorical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An implied author achieves various effects along different 'lines of interest' and can fall into pitfalls depending on commentary and narrator characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how commentary and narrator reliability/personalness interact with the chosen lines of interest to produce rhetorical effects. Use these interactions to judge whether the author's technical choices succeed or lead to unintended reader responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs telling is an inadequate absolute standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The rigid critical emphasis on distinguishing 'showing' from 'telling' is overly dogmatic; authors use both techniques according to rhetorical needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or writing fiction, do not treat 'showing' as inherently superior. Instead, examine why an author chooses showing or telling in service of rhetorical commitments and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial presence is inescapable
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to talk about a text without talking about an author because the existence of a text implies an author; readers will infer authorial beliefs and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how traces of authorial presence (even when indirect) shape interpretation; consider how the implied author influences perceived values, skill, and success of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric must be ethical; avoid 'rhetrickery'
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetoric ought not to be without ethics; 'rhetrickery' denotes shoddy, dishonest communicative arts that produce misunderstanding and harmful results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rhetorical acts for ethical quality: whether they mislead, exploit, or create misunderstanding. Writers and rhetors should listen to and consider audience welfare and strive to protect audiences against unethical persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of rhetoric: Win-Rhetoric, Bargain-Rhetoric, Listening-Rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth distinguishes types of rhetoric (Win-, Bargain-, and Listening-Rhetoric) and further sub-kinds, highlighting different aims and strategies in rhetorical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which type of rhetoric a work or rhetor employs and judge appropriateness: e.g., whether the aim is merely to win, to negotiate, or to engage in genuine listening and mutual understanding. Rhetors should moderate arguments by anticipating what is heard and by attending to audience welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric as the art of finding warrantable beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: In Modern Dogma and the Rhetoric of Assent Booth defines rhetoric as the art of finding warrantable beliefs and examines when one should change one's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate argumentative and persuasive moves by whether they produce warrantable (justifiable) beliefs and whether they engage opposing systems of belief constructively rather than simply reprinting them without engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of fiction: relocate ethics to the center
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth argues (in The Company We Keep) for relocating ethics to the center of engagement with literature — assessing literature's ethical effects and obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging fiction, consider ethical dimensions and the moral consequences of rhetorical strategies; literary evaluation should include how a work influences readers' ethical understanding and behavior.
